sections.title: Nominative Case (Subject)
sections.rule: The nominative is the dictionary form and marks the subject — who or what performs the action. Russian has no articles (no 'a'/'the'), so the bare noun stands alone. The verb 'to be' is dropped in the present, so a nominative noun can be a whole predicate.
sections.example_ref: English: The cat is sleeping on the sofa. / This is my sister.
sections.note: KOT speet na dee-VA-nye. Nominative answers кто?/что? (who?/what?). It is the only case with no preposition ever attached to it.

sections.title: Accusative Case (Direct Object)
sections.rule: The accusative marks the direct object of a transitive verb. Feminine -а/-я nouns change to -у/-ю (книга→книгу). Inanimate masculine and neuter nouns look like the nominative; animate masculine nouns copy the genitive.
sections.example_ref: English: I am reading a book. / He loves his dog.
sections.note: ya chee-TA-yu KNEE-gu. Ask кого?/что? (whom?/what?). Animacy matters: 'I see the man' = Я вижу человека (genitive-like ending).

sections.title: Genitive Case (Of / Absence)
sections.rule: The genitive shows possession ('of'), quantity, and the absence of something after нет. Typical endings: masculine/neuter -а/-я, feminine -ы/-и. It also follows у for 'have' and prepositions like после, без, из.
sections.example_ref: English: I have no time. / This is my brother's house.
sections.note: oo mee-NYA nyet VRYE-mye-nee. Ask кого?/чего? After нет the thing that is missing is ALWAYS genitive.

sections.title: Dative Case (To / For Someone)
sections.rule: The dative marks the recipient — to or for whom. Endings: masculine/neuter -у/-ю, feminine -е. Used for giving, and for feelings expressed as 'to me it is...' (мне нравится, мне холодно).
sections.example_ref: English: I gave her flowers. / I like this city.
sections.note: mnye NRA-vee-tsa. Ask кому?/чему? Many state expressions are dative: мне холодно = 'to-me [it is] cold' = I am cold.

sections.title: Instrumental Case (With / By Means Of)
sections.rule: The instrumental marks the tool used, and follows с for accompaniment ('together with'). Endings: masculine/neuter -ом/-ем, feminine -ой/-ей. It also names a profession after работать and follows быть in the past/future.
sections.example_ref: English: I write with a pen. / He works as a doctor.
sections.note: ya pee-SHOO ROOCH-koy. Note the difference: ручкой (no с) = the instrument; с другом = 'with a friend' (company).

sections.title: Prepositional Case (Location)
sections.rule: The prepositional never appears without a preposition. With в/на it means location ('in/at'), and with о it means 'about'. The usual ending is -е (в Москве, на столе, о работе).
sections.example_ref: English: I live in Moscow. / The book is lying on the table.
sections.note: ya zhee-VOO v mask-VYE. в = inside, на = on a surface or open place (на почте, на работе). Ask где?/о ком?

sections.title: Verb Aspect: Imperfective vs Perfective
sections.rule: Almost every Russian verb comes as a pair. The imperfective describes a process, habit, or repetition; the perfective describes a single completed action with a result. You must learn both forms together, e.g. читать/прочитать.
sections.example_ref: English: I was reading the book all evening. / I read (finished) the book in an hour.
sections.note: pra-chee-TAL. Perfective often adds a prefix (про-, на-, с-). Perfective has NO present tense — a 'present' perfective form is actually future.

sections.title: Present Tense Conjugation
sections.rule: Only imperfective verbs have a present tense. First-conjugation verbs take -ю/-ешь/-ет/-ем/-ете/-ют (читаю); second-conjugation take -ю/-ишь/-ит/-им/-ите/-ят (говорю). The verb быть ('to be') is simply omitted.
sections.example_ref: English: We speak Russian. / She cooks well.
sections.note: mih ga-va-REEM pa-ROO-skee. The ending shows the person, so pronouns are often optional in speech.

sections.title: Past Tense (Gender Agreement)
sections.rule: The past tense drops -ть and adds -л (m.), -ла (f.), -ло (n.), or -ли (pl.). It agrees with the subject's GENDER and number, not the person — so 'I read' differs for a man and a woman.
sections.example_ref: English: He was reading, and she was writing. / We lived in Kyiv.
sections.note: on chee-TAL, a a-NA pee-SA-la. A woman says я читала; a man says я читал — same word 'я', different ending.

sections.title: Future Tense (Two Types)
sections.rule: Imperfective future is compound: буду/будешь/будет + infinitive (я буду читать = I will be reading). Perfective future looks like the present but means completed future (я прочитаю = I will read [and finish]).
sections.example_ref: English: Tomorrow I will be working. / I will read the letter and reply.
sections.note: BOO-du ra-BO-tat. Rule of thumb: буду + infinitive = ongoing; single prefixed form = one finished result.

sections.title: Verbs of Motion
sections.rule: Motion verbs come in pairs: unidirectional (one trip in progress) vs multidirectional (habitual/round trips). идти/ходить = go on foot; ехать/ездить = go by vehicle. Prefixes add direction: при- (arrive), у- (leave), в- (enter), вы- (exit).
sections.example_ref: English: I am walking to school (right now). / He often travels to Moscow.
sections.note: ya ee-DOO f SHKO-lu. идти = one specific trip now; ходить = generally/repeatedly go. Choosing the wrong one is the classic learner error.

sections.title: Numbers and Case Agreement
sections.rule: Numbers govern the case of the noun. 1 (and any number ending in 1) takes the nominative singular; 2, 3, 4 take the genitive singular; 5 and above (and 11–14) take the genitive plural.
sections.example_target: У меня два брата и пять сестёр.
sections.example_ref: English: I have two brothers and five sisters. / There are three books on the table.
sections.note: dva BRA-ta, pyat see-STYOR. Two/three/four = 'genitive singular' (два стола); five+ = 'genitive plural' (пять столов).

sections.title: Comparatives and Superlatives
sections.rule: Form the comparative with -ее/-ей (быстрее = faster) or with более + adjective. The superlative uses самый + adjective (самый большой = the biggest). Common irregulars: лучше (better), хуже (worse), больше (more).
sections.example_ref: English: This road is shorter. / This is the most interesting film.
sections.note: ka-RO-che, SA-myy. 'than' is чем (+ nominative) or the genitive alone: Она выше меня = She is taller than me.

sections.title: Reflexive Verbs (-ся / -сь)
sections.rule: Reflexive verbs add -ся after a consonant and -сь after a vowel. They can be truly reflexive (мыться = wash oneself), reciprocal (встречаться = meet each other), or simply lexical (учиться = study, нравиться = be pleasing).
sections.example_ref: English: I study at university. / We are meeting at seven o'clock.
sections.note: ya oo-CHOOS. The particle attaches: учу-сь (after 'у'), учит-ся (after 'т'). It never takes a direct accusative object.

sections.title: Imperative Mood (Commands)
sections.rule: Build the imperative from the present stem: add -й after a vowel (читай), -и after a stressed consonant (говори), or -ь in some cases (будь). Add -те for the polite/plural form (читайте).
sections.example_ref: English: Speak more slowly, please. / Don't be late!
sections.note: ga-va-REE-tye. Use imperfective for polite invitations/repeated acts (Садитесь!) and perfective for a specific one-off request (Скажите...).

sections.title: Short-Form Adjectives
sections.rule: Short-form adjectives are used only as predicates (after an implied 'to be') and express a temporary state. They agree in gender/number but not case: он болен, она больна, они больны.
sections.example_ref: English: She is busy today. / This is very important.
sections.note: a-NA see-VOD-nya za-nya-TA. Long form = a permanent trait (больной человек = a sick person); short form = a current state (он болен = he is [now] ill).

sections.title: Possessives and свой
sections.rule: Possessives мой/твой/наш/ваш agree with the possessed noun in gender, number and case. The reflexive свой means 'one's own' and always refers back to the subject of the clause, replacing his/her/their when the owner is the subject.
sections.example_ref: English: She loves her (own) job. / Take your things.
sections.note: svah-YU ra-BO-tu. Она любит её работу = she loves HER (someone else's) job; свою = her own. его/её/их never change form.

sections.title: Conditional / Subjunctive with бы
sections.rule: To express 'would' or an unreal condition, use the past-tense verb + the particle бы. For hypothetical 'if' clauses use если бы + past, and the result clause also takes бы + past.
sections.example_target_2: Если бы у меня было время, я бы пришёл.
sections.example_ref: English: I would like a coffee. / If I had time, I would come.
sections.note: ya kha-TYEL by KO-fye. There is only one conditional form — the past + бы covers 'would', 'would have', and 'if...would'. бы can move around the clause.

sections.title: Purpose Clauses with чтобы
sections.rule: чтобы means 'in order to' / 'so that'. If the subject is the same in both clauses, use чtoby + infinitive. If the subjects differ, use чтобы + past-tense verb.
sections.example_ref: English: I study in order to know more. / I want you to come.
sections.note: CHTO-by znat. Same subject → infinitive; different subject → past tense. After verbs of wishing (хотеть) the second-subject construction is required.

sections.title: Negative Pronouns with ни-
sections.rule: Negative words никто (nobody), ничто (nothing), никогда (never), нигде (nowhere) REQUIRE the verb to also be negated with не. Russian uses obligatory double (multiple) negation.
sections.example_ref: English: I don't know anyone. / He is never late.
sections.note: ya nee-ka-VO nye ZNA-yu. Both negatives are mandatory: dropping the не is a grammar error. Prepositions split ни: ни у кого, ни о чём.

sections.title: Participles (причастия)
sections.rule: Participles are verbal adjectives that decline like adjectives and agree with their noun. Present active: -ущ/-ющ/-ащ (читающий = who is reading). Past passive: -нн/-т (прочитанный = [that has been] read).
sections.example_ref: English: The man reading the newspaper is my father. / This is the letter written yesterday.
sections.note: chee-TA-yu-shchiy. Mostly formal/written Russian. Passive participles often shorten as predicates: письмо написано = the letter is written.

sections.title: Verbal Adverbs (деепричастия)
sections.rule: A verbal adverb describes a secondary action by the same subject. The imperfective -я form shows a simultaneous action (читая = while reading); the perfective -в form shows a prior action (прочитав = having read).
sections.example_ref: English: While reading the book, he took notes. / Having read the letter, she smiled.
sections.note: chee-TA-ya. Both actions must share ONE subject. It is invariable — it never changes for gender, number or case.
